4.2.17 Waste heat
The heat generated from conversion losses of the electrolysers and/or the fuel cell stacks, i.e. from their cooling systems. This heat can be supplied to a local consumer within the renewable energy hub (e.g., a building, a greenhouse, a drying facility, etc.) and/or exported to a district heating (DH) network.
In the case of local heat consumption, any excess heat that cannot be absorbed by the consumer is considered wasted. If there is not enough heat produced by electrolysers and fuel cell stacks, additional heat must be purchased from the current heating source at its regular price. Therefore, the waste heat is effectively lowering current spending on heating requirements.
When heat is sold to a DH network, the model assumes no export limit by default. However, a limit can be imposed if the DH network cannot accept large amounts of heat.
The temperature level of both the local consumption and DH connection is assumed to be the same.
For more flexible heat delivery, the system includes a thermal energy storage (TES) unit.
If low-temperature heat must be upgraded to supply a high-temperature demand, a heat pump is required, which operates using electricity.
Heat from the electrolyser(s) and fuel cell stack(s) is delivered through low-temperature and high-temperature heat exchangers. These represent the complete heating subsystem, including pipes, valves, pumps, and control equipment.
Heat flows are automatically balanced by the optimization model between local consumption, TES, and DH export.

4.2.18 Waste treatment plant
The Waste treatment plant (WT) converts waste into hydrogen, electrical energy and heat. The plant consists of one or more reactors, each with its own process, technical and financial parameters. The tool determines the optimal size of every reactor, expressed as the amount of waste it can treat per day [t/day].
Besides hydrogen, the waste treatment process produces several by-products:

Electrical energy – the reactor can produce or consume electricity, depending on the process. Net production is fed to the electrical bus of the hub, while net consumption is supplied by the other electricity sources.
Heat – high- and low-temperature heat that can be used by the Waste heat component.
Carbon black – solid carbon that is sold to the market and generates revenue.
Tar – a by-product that must be disposed of, which causes an operating cost.
CO2 – emissions that are paid for at the CO2 emission price.

The waste for the reactors comes from the Waste source and storage component, which is enabled automatically together with the waste treatment plant.






Important



Hydrogen from the waste treatment plant is not green hydrogen. It is always counted as non-green hydrogen in the hydrogen balance and cannot be used to satisfy green hydrogen demand. In the same way, the electricity consumed by the reactors is supplied by non-green sources unless green electricity is available.


Operation of reactors
The waste treatment process is modelled with a daily time resolution. Reactors are assumed to operate continuously at their full installed capacity, i.e. every reactor treats an amount of waste equal to its size in every hour it is available. Availability is reduced only by planned maintenance and the following heating (start-up) period:

At the maintenance start date, the reactor stops and treats no waste for the maintenance duration (in days).
On the first day after the maintenance, at the start time of the reactor (hour of the day), the reactor starts preheating.
During the starting duration (in hours), the reactor still treats no waste, but it consumes additional electricity – the starting electricity consumption surge. The surge is proportional to the reactor size and is modelled with the electrical time step, so it appears as a short peak in electricity consumption.
After the preheating, the reactor returns to full operation.

The maintenance happens on the same date every year of the simulation. If a day is only partially affected by the maintenance (e.g. the day when the preheating ends), the reactor treats proportionally less waste in that day. If the maintenance duration is 0, there is no maintenance and no starting surge.
The outputs of a reactor are defined with the process matrix. Each output (electricity, heat, hydrogen, carbon black, tar, CO2) is calculated from the treated amount of waste and its composition (mass fractions of hydrogen, carbon and water defined in the Waste source and storage component), e.g. for electricity:
\[
P_\mathrm{el} = \dot{m}_\mathrm{waste} \cdot \left( \beta_\mathrm{H2,el}\,\omega_\mathrm{H2} + \beta_\mathrm{C,el}\,\omega_\mathrm{C} + \beta_\mathrm{H2O,el}\,\omega_\mathrm{H2O} \right)
\]
where \(\beta\) are the process coefficients of the reactor and \(\omega\) are the mass fractions of the waste.
Use of produced hydrogen
Hydrogen from the reactors is compressed and stored in the hydrogen tank, from where it can be used by the Fuel cell stack or sold through H2 sales. If neither of these components is enabled, the hydrogen produced by waste treatment is released into the atmosphere.

No reactor defined: at least one reactor must be added, otherwise the optimization cannot start.

Otherwise, the validation reports an error or the optimization becomes infeasible. In that case, increase the demand for non-green hydrogen, or decrease the existing or minimum reactor size.




4.2.19 Waste source and storage
The Waste source and storage (WSS) component defines how much waste is available to the Waste treatment plant, what its composition is, and how it can be stored before treatment. It does not have its own checkbox – it is enabled automatically together with the waste treatment plant.
Waste source
The waste source is defined by the amount of waste available over the year. The waste can be given as monthly amounts or imported as a profile with daily, weekly or monthly values. Since the waste treatment is modelled with a daily resolution, the tool splits the available waste into days of the simulation. Monthly and weekly amounts are considered to arrive evenly through the whole month or week.
The energy hub is paid a waste treatment remuneration for every tonne of waste it takes. By default, the optimization takes only the amount of waste that pays off. If Treat all waste is selected, all available waste must be taken and treated.
Waste storage
The waste storage decouples the arrival of waste from its treatment. Waste that is taken but not treated in a day is stored and can be treated in later days, e.g. during periods with less available waste or after the maintenance of the reactors. The optimization determines the optimal storage capacity. The amount of stored waste at the end of the simulation must be the same as at its beginning, so the operation can be repeated every year.

4.2.20 LOHC components
Liquid organic hydrogen carriers (LOHC) allow hydrogen to be stored and transported in liquid form. The LOHC components form two streams. The export stream (LOHC sales with its hydrogenation unit → LOHC tank) loads hydrogen produced on site into the carrier and sells the loaded LOHC; it requires the Electrolyser. The import stream (LOHC purchase with its dehydrogenation unit → LOHC tank) buys loaded LOHC and releases its hydrogen on site; it is always available. The released hydrogen can be used by H2 sales, the Fuel cell or the fixed hydrogen consumption, so LOHC import can be used without the Electrolyser. Only one stream can be active at a time. The stream is selected with the LOHC export / LOHC import checkboxes: checking one unchecks the other. The LOHC components are shown under three headers: LOHC sales (including the hydrogenation unit), LOHC purchase (including the dehydrogenation unit) and LOHC tank, which is used by both streams.
Hydrogen produced or released on site goes through the low-pressure hydrogen bus (see Section 4.2.12). The hydrogenation unit takes hydrogen from the bus, and the dehydrogenation unit delivers hydrogen to it.

4.2.20.1 LOHC sales
The LOHC sales component represents selling loaded LOHC to one or more customers. Each customer has a daily demand and a price, and may require green hydrogen. When loaded LOHC is delivered, the customer returns the same amount of unloaded LOHC. LOHC is sold only during the daily sales window, and the demand is satisfied only if it is economically viable. All quantities are expressed as mass of bound hydrogen.
The hydrogen is bound to the LOHC on site by the hydrogenation unit, which is defined in the Hydrogenation unit (advanced) section at the bottom of this component.
The component is part of the LOHC export stream and is shown only when the LOHC export checkbox is checked (see Section 4.2.20).

Heat released per kg of hydrogen bound to the LOHC (exothermic reaction, approx. 150–200 °C). It is set automatically when the carrier is chosen in the LOHC tank. Default: 8.11 kWh/kg (3,5-dibenzyl toluene).

Share of the reaction heat that can be recovered as high-temperature heat. Heat that is not recovered is removed by cooling, whose cost is neglected. Default: 97.5 %.

Share of the carrier that degrades during one hydrogenation. Lost carrier is replaced by buying make-up LOHC at the price given in the LOHC tank. Default: 0.02 %, i.e. 20 % of a total degradation of 0.1 % per cycle (range 0–0.04 %).

A time step belongs to the window if its interval overlaps the window, e.g. with a 24 h sampling time every day is in the window, and with a 4 h sampling time and a window from 8:00 until 20:00, the time steps starting at 8:00, 12:00 and 16:00 are in it.

LOHC tank, which supplies the unloaded LOHC to the hydrogenation unit, stores the loaded LOHC until it is sold, receives the returned unloaded LOHC and defines the carrier (and with it the reaction heat).
Electrolyser or the waste treatment plant (WT), which produce the hydrogen fed to the hydrogenation unit. LOHC export is available only when at least one of them is selected. Hydrogen from waste treatment is non-green, so it can only be sold to customers that accept non-green hydrogen.



4.2.20.1.5 Troubleshooting
Common issues and solutions:

LOHC export checkbox not visible: LOHC export requires the Electrolyser or WT. Select one of them first. Unchecking the last of them also unchecks LOHC export.
No customers configured: Add at least one customer before running the optimization.
Duplicate customer names: Each customer must have a unique name.
Invalid daily demand: The daily demand of every customer must be greater than zero.
Invalid price: The selling price must be greater than or equal to zero.
Invalid sales window: The start and end must satisfy 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 24.
Green hydrogen requirement: When Green hydrogen only is checked, ensure sufficient renewable energy sources are configured in the system.
Invalid hydrogenation unit sizes: The existing, minimum and maximum sizes of the hydrogenation unit must be greater than or equal to zero, and the minimum size must not be greater than the maximum size.
Invalid hydrogenation unit technical parameters: The specific electricity consumption and the reaction heat must be greater than or equal to zero. The hydrogen utilization must be greater than 0 % and at most 100 %, the recoverable share of reaction heat must be between 0 % and 100 %, and the LOHC loss must be at least 0 % and less than 100 %.
Invalid hydrogenation unit financial parameters: All prices must be greater than or equal to zero, the lifetime must be at least 1 year, and the subsidy must be between 0 % and 100 %.
Nothing is sold: Check that the selling price is higher than the cost of producing and loading the hydrogen, and that the customer’s daily demand is greater than zero. Green customers can only be served with green hydrogen.





4.2.20.2 LOHC purchase
The LOHC purchase component represents buying loaded LOHC from one or more suppliers. Each supplier has a daily availability and a price, and may supply green hydrogen. When loaded LOHC is delivered, the same amount of unloaded LOHC is returned to the supplier. Bought LOHC is stored in the LOHC tank and dehydrogenated on site. LOHC is bought only during the daily purchase window, and only if it is economically viable. All quantities are expressed as mass of bound hydrogen.
The hydrogen is released from the LOHC on site by the dehydrogenation unit, which is defined in the Dehydrogenation unit (advanced) section at the bottom of this component.
The component is part of the LOHC import stream and is shown only when the LOHC import checkbox is checked (see Section 4.2.20).

Parameter
Description

Last hydrogen use cannot be unchecked: While LOHC import is selected, at least one of H2 cons., Fuel cell or H2 sales must stay selected. Checking LOHC import selects H2 sales automatically if none of them is selected yet.

4.2.20.3 LOHC tank
The LOHC tank stores the liquid organic hydrogen carrier (LOHC). A single tank stores both unloaded and loaded LOHC, separated by a flexible membrane, so the amount of carrier in the tank is constant. The tank size is the mass of hydrogen it holds when all of its LOHC is loaded [kg]. The investment includes the tank and the first fill of the carrier.
The LOHC tank is also where the carrier is chosen. The carrier defines the hydrogen weight capacity, the carrier price and the reaction heat of the hydrogenation unit of LOHC sales.
The component is used by both LOHC streams and is shown when either the LOHC export or the LOHC import checkbox is checked (see Section 4.2.20).

4.2.21 Financial parameters
The Financial parameters component defines the economic constraints and incentives that apply to the entire hydrogen infrastructure project. These global financial settings affect the optimization of all components in the system.
This component is always present in the system and does not require any component selection checkbox. It contains settings for investment constraints, subsidies, and project lifetime.

4.2.21.1 Input parameters
Investment constraints
The investment constraints section allows you to set limits on the project’s payback period and total investment amount. These constraints help guide the optimization towards economically viable solutions.







Parameter
Description




Limit the payoff period?  [checkbox]
If enabled, the optimization will constrain the payback period to be within the specified maximum. If a lower bound on the size of any component is set to > 0, then this should be automatically turned off to ensure the feasibility of the optimization problem.


Maximum payback period  [years]
The longest acceptable timeframe (in years) for the project’s cumulative savings to offset the initial investment. This parameter is only visible if Limit the payoff period? is enabled.


Limit the investment amount?  [checkbox]
If enabled, the optimization will constrain the total investment to be within the specified maximum. If a lower bound on the size of any component is set to > 0, then this should be automatically turned off to ensure the feasibility of the LP solution.

The highest total amount (in €) you’re willing to invest in the project. This parameter is only visible if Limit the investment amount? is enabled.

Parameter

Common issues and solutions:

4.2.22 Simulation parameters
Simulation parameters control the simulation period, time resolution and solver settings used in the mathematical model. The simulation parameters are always present and must be configured for each scenario.

4.2.22.1 Input parameters
Time settings







Parameter
Description




Simulation start date  [date picker]
Starting day of the simulation period. If the simulation period is shorter than a year, all profiles (demands, consumptions, prices, etc.) are repeated until the whole year is fulfilled. The maximum duration is 365 days.


Simulation end date  [date picker]
The last day of the simulation period. If the simulation period is shorter than a year, all profiles (demands, consumptions, prices, etc.) are repeated until the whole year is fulfilled. The maximum duration is 365 days.



Sampling settings







Parameter
Description




Sampling time - electrical part  [h] (dropdown)
The sampling time for the purely electrical components of the hub: electrical grid connection, LREP, PV system, Wind farm, BESS, and electrical consumption. This sampling time must be less than or equal to the sampling time for hydrogen and heat. Common values are 1 hour (default), 2 hours, or 4 hours. With lower sampling time comes greater accuracy, but the price is greater computational complexity.


Sampling time - hydrogen and heat  [h] (dropdown)
The sampling time for H2 and heat components of the hub: water supply, electrolyser, fuel cell, waste heat. This sampling time must be greater than or equal to the sampling time for electrical part. Common values are 1 hour, 2 hours, 4 hours, or 24 hours. H2 and O2 sales have a fixed sampling time of 24 hours. With lower sampling time comes greater accuracy, but the price is greater computational complexity.



Optimization settings







Parameter
Description




Solver optimality tolerance  [-]
Both primal and dual feasibility tolerance. A lower value means more precise optimization but may require longer computation time. Default value is 1e-07.


Optimization timeout  [min]
The maximum time within which the optimization can be performed. If an optimal solution can be found within the solver optimality tolerance before the timeout is reached, the Results screen will be shown. Otherwise, a timeout error message will be displayed. Default value is 60 minutes.





4.2.22.2 Understanding time sampling
The sampling time determines the time resolution of the optimization model. There is a trade-off between accuracy and computational complexity:

Hourly sampling (1 hour): Provides the highest accuracy for modeling daily fluctuations in electricity prices, renewable generation, and demand. This is the default and recommended setting for most analyses.
2-4 hour sampling: Reduces computational time but may miss some short-term dynamics. Suitable for preliminary analyses or when investigating seasonal patterns.
Daily sampling (24 hours): Very fast but may not capture important intra-day effects. Typically used only for hydrogen part components which are modeled with daily resolution.

The electrical sampling time should always be less than or equal to the hydrogen/heat sampling time. The tool will automatically enforce this constraint.


4.2.22.3 Simulation period
The simulation period defines the time horizon for the optimization:

Full year (default): January 1 to December 31. All hourly profiles are used directly.
Partial year: Any period up to 365 days. If the period is shorter than a year, the profiles are repeated to fill the year. For example, if you simulate January to March, the model will repeat Q1 data for the remaining months.

The default simulation period is one full year (365 days).


4.2.22.4 Troubleshooting

Simulation duration too long: If the simulation period exceeds 365 days, an error message will be displayed. Reduce the simulation duration to a maximum of one (non-leap) year.
Optimization timeout: If the optimization does not complete within the specified timeout, consider:

Increasing the optimization timeout
Increasing the sampling time (e.g., from 1 hour to 2 hours)
Reducing the simulation period
Simplifying the system configuration by removing some components

Sampling time mismatch: If the electrical sampling time is greater than the hydrogen sampling time, the tool will automatically adjust the hydrogen sampling time to match.

title: 4  System structure
text:
4.3 Run optimization
After configuring all system components and their parameters, click Run optimization to generate the results. Once clicked, the tool performs the following sequence of operations:

Project save prompt

: The tool first asks whether you want to save the project before starting the optimization. You can choose to: - save the project,
- continue without saving, or
- cancel the optimization.
Saving the project is recommended in case an error occurs and the application closes unexpectedly.

Data validation

: The tool validates all parameters and their combinations to ensure they are within allowed ranges. If an invalid value is detected, a pop-up window titled Input validation failed appears. The message: - identifies the component where the issue occurs, and
- explains the reason for the failure.
Only the first detected issue is shown. After resolving it, run the optimization again to reveal any remaining issues.

Data processing

: The tool prepares all required inputs for the optimization, including: - obtaining profiles from online sources (PVGIS, renewables.ninja, Open-Meteo),
- scaling profiles according to user-defined values,
- generating and converting additional parameters (e.g., unit adjustments).
During this phase, additional validation is performed on the processed data.  
If validation fails here, the cause is usually:
- an incompatible combination of parameters, or  
- a temporary internet connectivity issue.

Problem generation

: After successful data preparation, the tool formulates the optimization problem and passes it to the solver.

Solving the problem

: The optimization problem is solved using the open-source HiGHS solver. When the solver finishes, one of the following status messages is displayed: - Successful optimization – the optimal solution was found.
- Time limit reached – a feasible but suboptimal solution was obtained.
- Unexpected error – the solver failed to complete.

Results post-processing

: After a successful run, the tool processes the results for presentation. A new window (Results) is created under the scenario tree node and automatically opened in the main workspace.

Waiting

During the entire procedure, a message Working, please wait… is displayed together with a loading indicator. While optimization is running:



the user interface is temporarily disabled,

no interaction is possible, and

the process cannot be stopped from within the application.

Stopping the optimization is planned for future releases. Currently, it can only be terminated via the system task manager.

Saving the data

Results are not saved automatically after optimization. Make sure to save the project manually to preserve the results.

title: 5  Results
text:
5.4 Financial results
The Financial Results section provides a comprehensive economic analysis of the optimized system.

5.4.1 Costs, revenues, and profits
This table presents the basic financial metrics:







Indicator
Description




Total investment cost (CAPEX)
The total upfront capital expenditure required to build the system, including all components and installation costs


Yearly operational cost (OPEX)
Annual operating expenses including maintenance, consumables, and variable costs


Yearly revenue
Annual income generated from selling hydrogen, oxygen, heat, or electricity


Yearly profit
Annual net profit defined as \(REVENUE - OPEX\)





5.4.2 Financial indicators
The financial indicators table provides advanced metrics for investment analysis.

5.4.2.1 Payback period
The payback period, also refered to as payoff period represents the time required for the cumulative cash flows from the investment to equal the initial capital expenditure.
Formula: \[N_{payoff} = \frac{CAPEX}{Profit_{total} - Profit_{exist}}\]
Where:

\(CAPEX\) = Total investment cost
\(Profit_{total}\) = Annual profit with the new system
\(Profit_{exist}\) = Annual profit from existing infrastructure only



5.4.2.2 Net present value (NPV)
NPV calculates the present value of all cash flows over the project lifetime, discounted at the specified rate. A positive NPV indicates that the investment is financially attractive.
Formula: \[NPV = -CAPEX + (Profit_{total} - Profit_{exist}) \times \frac{1 - (1+R)^{-N_{DL}}}{R}\]
Where:

\(R\) = Discount rate
\(N_{DL}\) = Project lifetime in years



5.4.2.3 Return on investment (ROI)
ROI expresses the total return on investment as a percentage over the project lifetime.
Formula: \[ROI = N_{DL} \times \frac{Profit_{total} - Profit_{exist}}{CAPEX} \times 100\%\]


5.4.2.4 Internal rate of return (IRR)
IRR is the discount rate that makes the NPV equal to zero. It represents the effective annual return on the investment. If the IRR exceeds your required rate of return, the investment is worthwhile.


5.4.2.5 Levelized cost of electricity (LCOE)
LCOE represents the average cost per unit of electricity produced by the system over its lifetime. It allows comparison with grid electricity prices or other generation technologies.
Formula: \[LCOE = \frac{PROFIT_{total\_without\_en} - PROFIT_{exist} - \frac{CAPEX}{N_{DL}}}{E_{consumed}} \times 1000\]
Unit: €/MWh

\(PROFIT_{total\_without\_en}\) stands for annual profit without cost of electricity in [€].
\(E_{consumed}\) stands for annual amount of electricity imported into the hydrogen hub in [kWh].



5.4.2.6 Levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH)
LCOH represents the average cost per kilogram of hydrogen delivered by the hub: sold (H2 sales and gas grid injection), sold bound to LOHC (LOHC sales), and used locally by the fixed hydrogen consumption. This is particularly useful for comparing hydrogen production costs from different technologies or against market prices.
Formula: \[LCOH = \frac{\frac{CAPEX}{N_{DL}} + PROFIT_{exist} - PROFIT_{total\_without\_H2}}{m_{H2,sold}}\]
Unit: €/kg

\(PROFIT_{total\_without\_H2}\) stands for annual profit without revenue from selling hydrogen (H2 sales, gas grid injection, LOHC sales) and without the savings of the fixed hydrogen consumption [€].
\(m_{H2,sold}\) stands for annual amount of hydrogen sold on the market, sold bound to LOHC, and used locally by the fixed hydrogen consumption in [kg].

5.14 Economic viability assessment
When evaluating the results, consider the following key indicators:

5.14.1 Primary decision metrics

Payback Period: How long until the investment pays for itself.
NPV: Whether the investment creates value

Positive NPV: Investment creates value
Negative NPV: Investment destroys value

IRR: The effective return on investment

Compare against your required rate of return or cost of capital




5.14.2 Secondary considerations

LCOE/LCOH: Compare against current market prices
Capacity factors: Higher utilization generally means better returns
Green hydrogen percentage: Important for sustainability goals and green hydrogen certifications
